triage.name: Diabetic Kidney Problems
triage.reason: Progressive albuminuria and declining kidney function; diagnosis reachable through history, labs and urine studies with a good differential.

demographics: More common in people with type 1 diabetes of long duration and type 2 diabetes
Higher rates in Black, Hispanic, Native American and South Asian populations
Often diagnosed in the primary care or diabetes clinic setting

risk_factors.text: Long-standing diabetes (10+ years for type 1, often shorter for type 2)
Family history of diabetic kidney disease or kidney failure

family_history: Diabetic kidney disease in a parent or sibling
Kidney failure requiring dialysis or transplant in a relative
social_history: Limited access to regular diabetes and blood pressure care

chief_complaints.text: My doctor says there is protein in my urine
My blood tests show my kidneys are not working as well
I have been throwing up and feeling sick

hpi.onset: Insidious; kidney damage begins years before any symptoms appear
hpi.duration: Usually detected after 5–15 years of diabetes, often at a routine screening visit
hpi.progression: Starts with small amounts of albumin in the urine (microalbuminuria), then progresses to heavier proteinuria and a gradual fall in glomerular filtration rate over years; symptoms appear only late
hpi.location: Kidneys; symptoms are systemic when they occur
hpi.quality: Usually asymptomatic; late symptoms are nonspecific tiredness, swelling and nausea
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate early; severe when kidney failure develops
relieving: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the feet, ankles or legs
Needing to urinate more often at night

pertinent_negatives: Recent sore throat or skin infection
Symptoms that started suddenly over days

argues_against: Primary heart failure as the only cause

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in the feet

negatives: Excessive thirst with very dilute urine

atypical.how_it_differs: People with type 2 diabetes may already have albuminuria or reduced kidney function at the time of diagnosis, because diabetes can be present for years before it is detected.
missing_classic_features: Long duration of known diabetes before kidney findings

atypical.how_it_differs: Reduced kidney function is often attributed to aging or hypertension, and symptoms are masked by other chronic illnesses.
When kidney function is already significantly reduced, symptoms of uremia such as nausea, itching, confusion and shortness of breath may dominate.
Protein in the urine and swelling can be mistaken for preeclampsia, and kidney function must be monitored closely.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may be overweight with stigmata of long-standing diabetes
general.moderate: Mildly fatigued, puffy eyelids or ankles, blood pressure elevated
general.severe: Ill-appearing, pale, sallow, with visible peripheral edema and scratch marks
general.critical: Lethargic or confused, markedly edematous, dyspneic, with uremic fetor

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff after 5 minutes of rest
findings.finding: Elevated blood pressure, often long-standing or poorly controlled hypertension

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area for 5 seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the feet, ankles or lower legs

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and gently press the periorbital skin
findings.finding: Periorbital puffiness, worst in the morning

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae and palmar creases
findings.finding: Conjunctival and palmar pallor suggesting anemia of chronic kidney disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk and extremities for excoriations
findings.finding: Excoriations and dry, sallow skin from uremic pruritus
Diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, exudates, neovascularization)

findings.maneuver: Test vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork and pinprick sensation on the feet
findings.finding: Reduced vibration or pinprick sensation from diabetic peripheral neuropathy

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular venous pulsation at 45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure from volume overload
Fine bibasilar crackles from pulmonary edema

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell
findings.finding: Third heart sound from volume overload

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both arms extended with wrists dorsiflexed for 30 seconds
findings.finding: Flapping tremor of the hands from uremic encephalopathy

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for masses and ballot the kidneys
findings.finding: No palpable abdominal or flank mass

findings.maneuver: Measure the temperature and inspect for a source of infection
findings.finding: No fever or focal infectious signs

labs.caveat: Rises only after substantial kidney function is lost; a normal creatinine does not exclude early diabetic kidney disease.
Also rises with dehydration and volume depletion, which are common in advanced disease.
Hyperkalemia is more likely with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or advanced kidney failure.
Metabolic acidosis from reduced acid excretion; worsens as kidney function declines.
Hyperphosphatemia appears in advanced disease and contributes to itching and bone disease.
Low calcium from reduced activation of vitamin D; check albumin to interpret total calcium.
Hypoalbuminemia from urinary protein loss and poor nutrition; also lowers total calcium.
Normocytic normochromic anemia from erythropoietin deficiency; worsens with kidney function.
Dipstick detects albumin but may miss light chains; a negative dipstick does not exclude early disease.
Glycosuria reflects hyperglycemia and is not by itself evidence of kidney damage.
Broad waxy casts suggest chronic kidney disease; RBC casts would point to a different glomerular disease.
Reflects glycemic control; less reliable in advanced kidney disease or anemia.
Dyslipidemia is common and adds cardiovascular risk.
Thyroid disease is more common in people with diabetes and can worsen kidney function.

findings.finding: Left ventricular hypertrophy (tall R waves, deep S waves, strain pattern)
Sinus rhythm; may become bradycardic or irregular with severe hyperkalemia

imaging.preferred_when: When another cause of kidney disease is suspected or kidney size is needed

findings.text: Bilateral small kidneys in advanced disease

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When a stone, mass, or structural cause is suspected and ultrasound is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Small, smooth kidneys with cortical thinning

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the renal arteries

findings.text: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the renal arteries

imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain, proteinuria is heavy or rapidly worsening, or a non-diabetic cause is suspected

findings.text: Mesangial expansion and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules)

initial.why: Assesses kidney function, potassium, bicarbonate and calcium
Looks for protein, glucose, casts and signs of another kidney process
Measures glycemic control, which drives progression
Looks for anemia of chronic kidney disease
Detects and quantifies albuminuria, the earliest marker of diabetic kidney disease
Excludes obstruction, stones or structural disease
initial.only_if: another cause of kidney disease is suspected or kidney size is needed

confirmatory.why: Confirms the diagnosis when the cause is uncertain or a non-diabetic disease is suspected
confirmatory.only_if: diagnosis is unclear, proteinuria is heavy or rapidly worsening, or another glomerular disease is suspected

supporting.why: Albumin, liver enzymes and total protein help assess nutrition and other causes
Cardiovascular risk is high and statins are often indicated
Thyroid disease is common in diabetes and can affect kidney function

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed unless a stone, mass or structural cause is suspected

not_indicated.test: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the renal arteries
not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected renovascular disease
No role in chronic kidney disease
Not helpful unless sepsis or hypoperfusion is suspected
Not helpful unless infection is suspected

decision_points: Confirm persistent albuminuria on two of three samples over 3 months before labeling diabetic kidney disease
Check for retinopathy; its presence supports diabetic kidney disease
Consider renal biopsy when the course is atypical, proteinuria is heavy or rapid, or another cause is suspected
Avoid NSAIDs and adjust medication doses for kidney function

criteria.name: Diabetic kidney disease (clinical)
criteria.summary: Persistent albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio generally 30 mg/g or higher) or reduced estimated GFR in a person with diabetes, with other causes of kidney disease excluded.
items: Persistent albuminuria on repeated testing or reduced estimated GFR
No other obvious cause of kidney disease

differential.name: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
differential.why_considered: Long-standing hypertension with slowly rising creatinine and mild proteinuria in the same patients who have diabetes

history: Long-standing hypertension, sometimes predating diabetes
Little or no albuminuria early on
No retinopathy
exam: Absence of diabetic retinopathy or neuropathy
labs: Mild proteinuria, usually well under 1 g/day
Bland urine sediment without waxy casts
imaging: Small kidneys with cortical thinning on ultrasound

differential.name: Nondiabetic glomerulonephritis
differential.why_considered: Proteinuria and declining kidney function in a person with diabetes can also come from a primary glomerular disease
differential.trigger: Heavy or rapidly worsening proteinuria, active urine sediment, or a course that does not fit diabetes

history: Recent upper respiratory or skin infection
Rash, joint pains or hemoptysis
Proteinuria that appeared suddenly rather than over years
exam: New hypertension or edema out of proportion to diabetes duration
labs: Active urine sediment with red blood cells and red blood cell casts
Low complement levels or positive autoantibodies
imaging: Renal biopsy shows immune complex or crescentic disease rather than diabetic changes

differential.name: Renal artery stenosis
differential.why_considered: Atherosclerosis is common in diabetes and can cause progressive kidney function loss with difficult-to-control hypertension
differential.trigger: Refractory hypertension, a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or flash pulmonary edema

history: Hypertension that is very hard to control
Creatinine rises after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Episodes of flash pulmonary edema
imaging: Magnetic resonance angiography or CT angiography shows narrowing of a renal artery

differential.name: Acute kidney injury from another cause
differential.why_considered: A sudden drop in kidney function in a patient with diabetes may be from dehydration, NSAIDs, contrast or obstruction rather than chronic diabetic kidney disease
differential.trigger: Creatinine rising over days rather than months, or a clear precipitant such as dehydration, NSAIDs or contrast

history: Recent vomiting, diarrhea or poor fluid intake
New NSAID, contrast or nephrotoxic medication
Symptoms starting over days
exam: Signs of volume depletion or obstruction
labs: Fractional excretion of sodium or urine sodium pattern suggesting prerenal or intrinsic injury
Bland sediment or muddy brown casts
imaging: Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis if obstruction is present

differential.name: Multiple myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy
differential.why_considered: Light-chain kidney disease can cause proteinuria and kidney failure in older adults
differential.trigger: Anemia, bone pain, hypercalcemia, or proteinuria with a negative urine dipstick for albumin

history: Bone pain, especially back or ribs
Recurrent infections
Fatigue and weight loss
labs: Anemia, hypercalcemia, elevated total protein with low albumin
Serum or urine protein electrophoresis with a monoclonal band
imaging: Skeletal survey or advanced imaging shows lytic lesions

differential.name: Urinary tract obstruction
differential.why_considered: Prostate enlargement or stones can cause rising creatinine and urinary symptoms in older patients with diabetes

history: Weak stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying
History of kidney stones
Recurrent urinary tract infections
imaging: Stone or bladder outlet obstruction on CT

differential.name: Diabetes insipidus
differential.why_considered: Both conditions involve diabetes and urination, and patients may confuse the two

history: Excessive thirst with large volumes of dilute urine
No proteinuria or kidney function decline
exam: Signs of dehydration if water access is limited
labs: Very dilute urine with low osmolality
Water deprivation test confirms the diagnosis

severity.mild: Early diabetic kidney disease: persistent microalbuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 30–300 mg/g) with normal or near-normal estimated GFR and no symptoms
severity.moderate: Established diabetic kidney disease: overt albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio above 300 mg/g), slowly rising creatinine, mild anemia, and early edema or hypertension
severity.severe: Advanced chronic kidney disease: estimated GFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², fluid overload, uremic symptoms such as nausea, itching and fatigue, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
severity.critical: End-stage kidney disease or a life-threatening complication such as severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, uremic pericarditis or uremic encephalopathy

red_flags.finding: Potassium above 6.0 mmol/L or ECG changes of hyperkalemia
red_flags.meaning: Life-threatening arrhythmia risk; needs urgent treatment

red_flags.finding: Severe shortness of breath with crackles and low oxygen saturation
red_flags.meaning: Pulmonary edema from volume overload; may need dialysis

red_flags.finding: Chest pain worse when lying down or a friction rub
Creatinine rising rapidly over days rather than months
red_flags.meaning: Suggests acute kidney injury or a non-diabetic kidney disease; needs urgent workup

red_flags.finding: Heavy proteinuria with active urine sediment or rapid decline
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a non-diabetic glomerular disease; consider biopsy

complications.name: Hyperkalemia
clues: Use of ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics

complications.name: Metabolic acidosis
clues: Low bicarbonate on basic metabolic panel

complications.name: Volume overload and pulmonary edema
clues: Shortness of breath when lying flat

complications.name: End-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplant
Cardiovascular disease
clues: Chest pain or shortness of breath

complications.name: Diabetic retinopathy and neuropathy
clues: Numbness or tingling in the feet

special_populations.differences: Reduced kidney function is often attributed to aging or hypertension; symptoms are masked by other chronic illnesses and medication doses need careful adjustment.
Proteinuria and swelling can be mistaken for preeclampsia; kidney function and blood pressure must be monitored closely, and ACE inhibitors and ARBs must be stopped.
Diabetic kidney disease is uncommon in children but can occur in adolescents with long-standing type 1 diabetes; screening should begin after puberty or 5 years of diabetes.
When kidney function is already significantly reduced, uremic symptoms dominate and medications must be dose-adjusted; avoid NSAIDs and certain contrast studies.
People with type 2 diabetes may already have albuminuria or reduced kidney function at the time of diagnosis, because diabetes can be present for years before it is detected.

key_questions.question: How long have you had diabetes, and what type?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing diabetes (10+ years for type 1); type 2 may already have kidney findings at diagnosis

key_questions.question: What have your recent blood sugar readings and HbA1c been like?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor glycemic control, which drives progression

key_questions.question: How well controlled is your blood pressure, and what are your usual readings?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypertension, a strong driver of kidney damage

key_questions.question: Have you been told there is protein or albumin in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent albuminuria, the earliest marker of diabetic kidney disease

key_questions.question: Have your kidney blood tests changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual rise in creatinine or fall in estimated GFR over months to years

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your feet, ankles or legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Peripheral edema from fluid retention or protein loss

key_questions.question: Is your urine foamy or bubbly?
Have you had any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or flank pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests infection, stones or another kidney process

key_questions.question: Do you take any pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAID use, which worsens kidney function

key_questions.question: Are you taking an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or an SGLT2 inhibitor?
Do you have any eye problems from diabetes, like retinopathy?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetic retinopathy, which supports diabetic kidney disease

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have kidney disease or need dialysis?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of diabetic kidney disease or kidney failure

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden severe symptoms like confusion, chest pain, or trouble breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis or pulmonary edema requiring urgent care

reasoning_points: Long-standing diabetes with poor glycemic control and hypertension
Persistent albuminuria on repeated testing or reduced estimated GFR
Presence of diabetic retinopathy or neuropathy supporting microvascular disease
Gradual decline in kidney function over months to years rather than days
Absence of active urine sediment, fever, flank pain or other features suggesting a non-diabetic cause
Other causes of kidney disease considered and excluded

easy: Long-standing type 1 diabetes with known microalbuminuria
Classic gradual rise in creatinine with hypertension and retinopathy
No red flags or atypical features
medium: Type 2 diabetes with albuminuria at diagnosis
Mildly reduced kidney function attributed to aging
hard: Rapidly worsening proteinuria suggesting non-diabetic glomerulonephritis
Creatinine rising over days from acute kidney injury or NSAIDs
Older adult with anemia, bone pain and proteinuria suggesting myeloma
Refractory hypertension with a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor suggesting renal artery stenosis
